messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rajiv, a 50-year-old South Asian man married for over two decades, has been an animator at a small studio in Los Angeles for almost three decades. His life took a sharp turn when his young son was diagnosed with a severe illness that nearly took his life several years ago. Since then, Rajiv's daily routine has become increasingly marred by intrusive thoughts and avoidance behaviors. One evening, while lying alone in an unfamiliar hotel room during a work trip, Rajiv felt an overwhelming sense of dread wash over him. The memory of the sterile hospital where his son spent weeks battling for his life suddenly loomed large in his mind. The antiseptic smell that lingered in the room triggered vivid flashbacks of the harrowing nights he and his wife had sat by their son’s bedside, watching the medical team work tirelessly to save him. Since that time, Rajiv has become acutely aware of specific triggers that send him spiraling into a cycle of rumination and reassurance-seeking. Sleeping alone or in unfamiliar places now feels intolerable; it reminds him too much of those nights in the hospital when he lay awake, counting the beeps of machines, waiting for any sign that his son might not make it through the night. Whenever Rajiv undergoes a medical examination or procedure at the clinic, the sterile environment sets off waves of anxiety. He finds himself mentally rehearsing worst-case scenarios to feel prepared, but this only heightens his distress. The olfactory trigger—the antiseptic smell—is especially potent, transporting him back to those desperate moments. To cope with these intrusive thoughts and feelings, Rajiv has turned to maladaptive strategies that provide temporary relief but ultimately exacerbate his anxiety. He often ruminates about how he could have prevented the situation or imagined ways to get even with fate for putting them through such a nightmare. This rumination leads him to seek constant reassurance from his wife and colleagues, asking repeatedly if they think everything will be okay. The more Rajiv engages in these maladaptive strategies, the more he becomes hypersensitive to his triggers. Each time he experiences a trigger, the cycle begins anew. For instance, after a routine check-up at the clinic where the antiseptic smell is unmistakable, he finds himself ruminating throughout the day and seeking reassurance from his wife multiple times. This vicious cycle has taken its toll on Rajiv’s work as an animator. His colleagues have noticed that he often seems distracted and withdrawn during meetings, frequently asking for clarifications or repeating questions to reassure himself of their safety protocols at the studio. The anxiety has also strained his relationship with his son, who now senses something is amiss but doesn't fully understand what his father is going through. What finally brought Rajiv to seek help was a particularly distressing night when he could not sleep alone and found himself ruminating all night about worst-case scenarios for his son’s health. He realized that the constant need for reassurance and the inability to cope with these triggers were affecting every aspect of his life. Despite his initial reluctance, Rajiv is now seeking help because he is most afraid of losing control over his thoughts and fears for his family's well-being. At the same time, he hopes to regain a sense of peace and normalcy in his daily life.
